ana_01.label: Dataset profile
ana_01.content: The dataset covers 178,749 repair attempts logged across 447 Repair Cafe branches in 25 countries between April 2015 and August 2026. Volunteers categorized items into 14 broad categories and 1,951 distinct kind_of_product values, manufactured by 8,600 distinct (volunteer-spelled) brands. The two CSVs are joinable on repair_id: repairs.csv carries the structured fields (date, country, product, brand, repaired status, repairability score) and repairs_text.csv carries the free-text fields (defect_found, problem_description, repair_method, failure_reasons, failure_reason_open, repair_info_source, suggestions).

ana_02.label: Repair outcome: 63% fully fixed, 76% at least partly fixed
ana_02.content: Across all 178,749 logged attempts, volunteers fully repaired the item 63.1% of the time (112,776 cases), partly repaired 12.8% (22,859), and could not repair 24.1% (43,112). Two rows lack a repaired flag and one Dutch row was tagged 'ja' (Dutch for 'yes') and is normalized into 'yes'. The combined yes-or-half success rate is 75.9%. This is slightly under the 65% headline statistic the foundation reported in 2018 for fully-successful repairs, suggesting Repair Cafes have, if anything, become slightly more successful over time as volunteer experience accumulates.

ana_03.label: Top 15 most-repaired product types
ana_03.content: Coffee makers (10,770) and vacuum cleaners (10,284) are the two items most often dragged in for repair, each comprising about 6% of all attempts. They are followed by trousers/pants (6,769), bicycles (4,887), and sewing machines (4,614). The top 15 product types are dominated by household electric appliances and basic textiles. The list confirms — and freshens with 2026 numbers — the foundation's 2018 finding that coffee machines, vacuums, and lamps were the three most common visitors.

ana_04.label: Success rate by product type — knives and trousers thrive, kettles and printers don't
ana_04.content: Repair success varies wildly by item. The clear winners are non-electric, mechanical items: knives/scissors are repaired 97.5% of the time (mostly sharpening), trousers/pants 96.0%, garden shears 95.4%, coats/jackets 89.7%, and bicycles 84.1%. The clear losers are electronics with sealed components or cheap consumer-grade builds: electric kettles succeed only 39.9% (50.9% are unfixable), printers 36.8% (42.2% unfixable), irons 49.4%, food processors 49.1%, laptops 49.7%, toasters 51.1%, and coffee makers 50.6%. The data tells a story: the more electronic the item, the less likely it can be saved.

ana_05.label: Country distribution: Netherlands dominates
ana_05.content: The Netherlands accounts for 50.8% of all logged repairs (90,839 of 178,749) — unsurprising since the movement was founded there in 2009. Great Britain follows with 21.1% (37,692), France with 11.0% (19,724), Canada 4.3%, Australia 4.0%. Together the top five countries account for 91.2% of all rows. Twenty other countries split the remaining 8.8%, with several (IE, IT, FI, NZ) having only a few hundred rows each. The Dutch over-representation is a major caveat for any global claim — Dutch coffee culture (the Senseo) almost certainly biases the 'most-repaired item' rankings.

data_table.description: Repairs logged by country (top 15).

ana_06.label: Yearly volume: 1,600x growth from 2015 to 2025
ana_06.content: Logged repairs grew from 28 in 2015 (the dashboard's first year) to 45,165 in 2025 — a 1,613x increase. Growth was steady through 2019 (15,491 logs), dropped to 6,686 in 2020 and 5,813 in 2021 (COVID closed cafes physically), then rebounded in 2022 (15,096) and accelerated to 29,406 (2023), 39,981 (2024), and 45,165 (2025). The 2026 figure of 7,346 reflects only the first eight months. The reach of the Repair Cafe movement, in other words, is a hockey stick — the data underestimates the early years because the dashboard didn't exist yet.

data_table.description: Repairs logged per year, 2015-2026 (2026 partial).

ana_07.label: Repairability score distribution (1-10)
ana_07.content: Volunteers rate each item on a 1 (difficult) to 10 (easy) repairability scale. The mean rating is 6.66 and the median 7. The distribution is bimodal-ish, peaking at 10 (22,424 items rated 'trivially easy'), 8 (21,766), and 7 (15,217), with a smaller secondary peak at 1 (8,557 items rated 'impossible'). Only 188 items got a 0 (a small data-entry quirk). The mode-of-bimodality reflects how Repair Cafe attempts split: most items either prove very fixable once a fixer looks at them, or are immediately recognized as not worth the time. Repairability is missing for 53,885 rows (30.1%) — typically when an attempt failed before a rating could be assigned.

data_table.description: Counts at each repairability score, 0-10.

ana_08.label: Category-level repair odds: textile thrives, electronics struggle
ana_08.content: Aggregating to the 14 high-level categories, textile leads on repair success at 92.3% (24,412 rows), followed by tools non-electric (90.0%) and jewelry (82.9%). At the bottom, display-and-sound equipment is repaired only 45.8% of the time (20,415 rows) and computer-equipment-and-phones 46.4% (9,488 rows). Household appliances electric, the largest category at 70,983 rows, sits at 55.3% — almost exactly mid-pack. The cleanest split in the data is electric vs non-electric: electric items succeed roughly half the time, non-electric items roughly nine times in ten.

ana_09.label: Top failure reasons: it's the parts, stupid
ana_09.content: Across the 65,999 failed-or-half-repaired records, volunteers selected from a checkbox list of failure reason tags. The most common tag is 'No way to fix the product' (5,544 cases, 8.4% of failures), followed by 'Spare parts not available at repair session' (4,694; 7.1%), 'Unidentified failure' (3,662; 5.5%), 'Too worn out' (3,341; 5.1%), and 'No way to open the product' (2,305; 3.5%). Spare-parts problems collectively (parts not available at session, not on market, or too expensive) account for 9,042 tags — the single largest barrier when grouped. This data confirms the foundation's earlier 2018 finding that parts availability is the dominant blocker and supports the EU Right-to-Repair argument that manufacturers must make spares accessible.

ana_10.content: The free-text defect_found field is multilingual (Dutch dominates because of NL volume, with French and German runners-up alongside English). Across languages and forms, the same six diagnoses recur: it doesn't work, it stopped working, it leaks, it's blunt, it's torn, it's broken.

ana_12.label: GenAI vs YouTube as repair information sources
ana_12.content: Volunteers can record where they got repair information. YouTube has been the dominant external source since 2017, but its share has plateaued: 0.3% in 2017, 0.5% in 2023, 0.4% in 2026 (early). Generative AI is a brand-new entrant — zero mentions before 2023 — but is rising fast on a relative basis: 2 mentions in 2023, 8 in 2024, 14 in 2025, and 2 in the partial 2026 sample. The earliest unambiguous AI mention is 9 September 2023 ('chat gpt' for an unspecified item). Examples of how volunteers logged it include 'chat gpt', 'WWW.OPENai.COM', 'chatgpt', 'AI Perplexity', 'perplexity et manuel', and even an OpenAI conversation share URL. While AI mentions remain a tiny fraction of total rows (26 cumulatively versus 843 YouTube mentions), the trajectory in this dataset is the first traceable evidence in volunteer repair logs of a new tool entering the fixer's toolkit.

ana_14.label: Where the parts run out: electric tools and household electrics top the spare-parts blocker
ana_14.content: Restricting to records flagged with a spare-parts failure tag, electric tools have the highest spare-parts blocker rate at 8.3% of all attempts (and 18.0% of all failed attempts in that category). Household appliances electric is second at 7.4% of attempts (16.5% of failed). Display and sound equipment is third at 6.3% / 11.7%. Textile, by contrast, has spare-parts blockers in only 0.5% of attempts — needles and thread are universally available. The pattern aligns with EU Right-to-Repair concerns: it is consumer electronics, not clothing or hand tools, where manufacturers' control of spare parts most directly translates into items being thrown away.

ana_15.label: Repairability score is a strong predictor of success
ana_15.content: There is a clear monotonic relationship between volunteer repairability rating and outcome. Items rated 1 ('difficult') are repaired only 13.7% of the time. The success rate climbs almost linearly to 56.9% at score 5, then 78.4% at 8, 84.9% at 9, and 85.8% at 10. The fact that even score-10 items fail 14% of the time tells you something else — sometimes a fixable item is not actually fixed because the volunteer ran out of time, lacked a part on the day, or the visitor never came back to collect the result. The score itself is a useful, internally-consistent signal of design quality.

ana_16.label: Brand of vacuum/coffee-maker matters: Dyson at the bottom
ana_16.content: Holding product type constant, brand-level success rates vary by 22 percentage points. For vacuum cleaners (n>=100 brand subset), Henry leads at 69.2% success, with Miele 66.0%, Siemens 65.4%, Philips 64.8%, AEG 63.1%. Dyson sits at the bottom at 47.4% (n=1,202) — a brand widely associated with premium price and proprietary design. For coffee makers, Philips (the Senseo manufacturer) leads at 59.5% (n=3,343), followed by Saeco 57.1% and De'Longhi 55.5%. Bosch coffee makers are the worst at 39.0% and Braun the worst overall at 30.9%. Sample sizes here are large enough that the cross-brand spread is unlikely to be noise — though all branding analysis is volunteer-spelled and Dyson units may also skew newer (and harder to open).

ana_17.label: Country-level success rate: Italy and Israel ahead, France behind
ana_17.content: Restricting to countries with at least 100 logged rows, Italy leads on full-success rate at 79.1% (n=139), followed by Israel 77.6% (n=1,559), Finland 76.6% (n=107), Ireland 75.6%, New Zealand 73.2%, US 70.9%. The Netherlands — where the movement was born and which hosts more than half the data — sits mid-pack at 62.3%. France brings up the rear at 55.6%, with Spain at 55.7% just ahead. The gap between top and bottom is 23 percentage points. Some of the difference reflects product mix (countries with more textile-heavy submissions look more successful) and some likely reflects how cafes log half-repairs versus full repairs locally.

data_table.description: Repair success rate by country (n>=100).

ana_18.label: Item-age vs success: a U-shape, with old items doing surprisingly well
ana_18.content: Plotting success rate against estimated item age reveals a U-shape. New items (0-1 years old) succeed 67.1% of the time — often simple defects under warranty issue. Then success drops to a trough around 6-10 years (55.9%) and 11-15 years (56.6%) — items with worn motors, dead capacitors, no spare parts. Then it rises again: 21-30 years 61.1%, 31-50 years 62.0%, 50+ years 63.2%. The vintage rebound makes physical sense: old items (sewing machines, clocks, radios) were built before planned obsolescence took hold, with replaceable parts and accessible internals. The dataset has 14,112 items aged 20+ years, dominated by sewing machines (1,212), clocks (553), vacuum cleaners (483), radios (471), and turntables (356).

data_table.description: Success rate by estimated item age bucket.

ana_19.label: Vintage items: 14,112 objects aged 20+ brought back from the dead
ana_19.content: Items aged 20 years or older — meaning they were built in or before the early 2000s — were brought to Repair Cafes 14,112 times, and 61.6% were successfully repaired. The categories that anchor this vintage flow are sewing machines (1,212 cases), clocks (553), vacuum cleaners (483), radios (471), turntables/record players (356), table lamps (340), and bicycles (331). These are the icons of pre-throwaway design: items that were expensive enough to be worth fixing, simple enough to be opened, and built with parts that are still findable. Vintage textile and lighting items in particular have very high success rates.

ana_22.label: Cumulative CO2 saved: 2,707 tonnes from this dataset alone
ana_22.content: Applying the Repair Cafe Foundation's 24-kg-CO2-per-successful-repair benchmark from det_03, the 112,776 successful repairs in this dataset prevented an estimated 2,707 tonnes of CO2 emissions from manufacturing replacements. This is one community sample — the foundation's network-wide estimate is far larger.

caveats.content: Netherlands rows account for 50.8% of the dataset (90,839 of 178,749). 'Most-repaired item' rankings reflect Dutch consumer culture (Senseo coffee makers, Henry vacuums) more than a global average.

Free-text fields are multilingual (Dutch, French, German, English). Phrase counts in any single language under-represent the same defect concept reported in another language; theme-level counts are more comparable.
Brand strings are volunteer-written: 'Chat GPT' / 'chatgpt' / 'CHAT GPT' all coexist; brand name spelling varies. AI-mention counts depend on whether volunteers wrote any of the search terms above.

Repairability score is missing for 30.1% of rows, often because the volunteer never finished assessing. Country/category averages of repairability are therefore biased toward items that got far enough into the process to be rated.
2026 covers only Apr-Aug at most; 2026 yearly numbers are partial and should not be compared directly to full years.
The 24-kg-CO2-per-repair figure is a single research estimate (Steve Privett, University of Surrey, master's thesis). Real-world CO2 savings vary by product type.
